title: [40k] Weekend Update: November 2, 2026
content:
In our Weekend Update series, we cover the big events and stories that are happening each week in wargames, so you can stay updated and informed every week. The 40k side will be mostly covered by me, Isaac Terada, while Dan “Swiftblade” Richardson covers the non-40k side of event coverage and news. 

Talavera Caps Off Weekend Big for Teams, Light for Singles

October ended with a surprising weekend that held only a single qualifying event in our sample - we typically only look at events with 5+ rounds and 28 players when we define our GT+ events - with only a single qualifying singles event for the weekend. Instead competitive 40k was dominated by teams events, headlined by the Talavera GT, a massive, 804-player teams event held in Talavera de la Reina, Spain, which marked the largest teams event of the year. This skew's the week's stats a little bit when it comes to understanding shifts in the meta, but you can rest assured that bikes and land speeders were still major factors globally.

Speaking of teams events...

Wargames Adictos Wins Year's Largest Teams Event

It was a particularly big weekend for six-man teams events, with Talavera and Super 6 both offering opportunities for teams of 6 to square off. The largest of these - and the year's biggest teams event (and also in contention for the year's biggest event) - was in Talavera, with 804 players split among 134 teams of six. The event itself was six rounds, leading to four undefeated teams at the end of the weekend, though ultimately Team Wargames Adictos won on points with a least featuring World Eaters (Recon), Imperial Knights (Purge), Necrons (Priority), Dark Angels (T&H), Orks (Disruption), and Thousand Sons (Priority).

Congratulations to:

  •  Gonzalo "Raven" de La Moneda
  •  Juanma Joker
  •  Manu
  •  Marco Esteban
  •  Miguel Durá
  •  Terroxer El Rojo

for winning the event, with an additional acknowledgement for Team Euskadi, 3 Arpía, and Cónclave for finishing with undefeated records.

Team England Takes October Super 6’s Crown

The weekend's next largest teams event featured only a measly 144 players duking it out over five rounds with six-player teams. Team England won the event with a 5-0 record, edging out Team Morocco for the top spot.

Congrats to:

  • Danny Evison
  • Harley Scully
  • Mani Cheema
  • Mike Porter
  • Tony Chew
  • Will B

Xenofilerna Omega Wins TTT 2026

The weekend's third big European event, team Xenofilerna Omega won this five-round, four-man teams event featuring 96 players.

Congrats to:

  • Benjamin Hyvönen
  • Björn Eriksson
  • Jacob Edvinsson
  • Johan Edvinsson

黑石要塞 Wins the South China Open

The final large teams event of the weekend was the South China Open, another 6-man teams event with four rounds and 84 total players. Team 黑石要塞 (which I believe translates to “Blackstone Fortress”) won the event with a 3-1-1 record.

Congrats to:

  • Bill Zuda
  • eddy E
  • 杂耍 Z
  • 白给 Wade
  • 老陈 C
  • 萝卜 L

Dylan Cowan Wins Weekend's Largest Singles 40k Event

The lone qualifying singles event this past weekend was the Calling the Banners 2026 event in Coburg North, Australia. This 67-player, 5-round event was conquered by Dylan Cowan, who won the event piloting a Dark Angels Take and Hold List running Assault Brethren, Darkflight Pursuit, Stormlance Task Force, and a ton of Outriders and Land Speeders.

Funny Thing About Statistics…

Actually I think Deathwatch might be bad; no one even played them this weekend. Necrons also had a record low 26% win rate. Well, this might be because we tracked a single GT event this weekend of just 67 players. Tracking win rates in teams tends to throw off data since the pairings process can lead to some factions having unnaturally high or low win rates. Tune in next week where we will hopefully have much more relevant results to study.

The ITC Is Dead! Long Live the WGR!

The ITC has been an integral part of the 40K scene for a very long time, much longer then my personal 40K career. Players who have been following the scene will have noticed that the ITC changed hands a few years ago, moving from its previous owners at Frontline Gaming to Games Workshop as part of the new World Championships program. Earlier this year Games Workshop finally chose to scuttle the ITC, renaming the ranking system to the Warhammer Global Rankings. Over the weekend Best Coast Pairings put out a social post on Facebook alluding to new scoring in the new season, starting after this year's World Championships, though no changes appear to have been announced or planned at this time.

I am sure many people can remember a time where Games Workshop did not care about competitive 40K; those days are certainly gone and I am excited to see where they continue to grow in how they mange the 40K competitive scene.

Photo Credit: Mani Cheema

Player Focus: Mani Cheema

As the 2026 World Championships rapidly approach, we'll look at the top players on the WGR leaderboards to see who can have a chance to take home the crown. We already covered spots #1 and #3 over the past weeks so let’s look to spot #2. Mani Cheema is a veteran player well known in the UK scene and currently second in the ITC, with a top teams finish this past weekend at the Super 6s event. Mani previously won the World Championships in 2023 and I'd be shocked if he didn't make a deep run at the crown again this year. Mani is a jack-of-all trades player: You’ll never know what he might be on, though he's often seen running powered-armoured Chaos warriors, such as with this past weekend's Death Guard list.

Alongside our coverage of the what's-what of 40k each week, Dan “Swiftblade” Richardson joins us to provide some quick updates on the movers and shakers in the competitive scene of some of the other games we cover here at Tabletop Battles!

Khazalite Holds Clanshields - Credit Mildnorman

Khazalite Holds Release over the Weekend; Wave Two Up for Preorder

It’s been a dwarf-heavy episode over in the Mortal realms, as the new Khazalite Holds faction has been front and center for Age of Sigmar since its announcement at the big autumn preview. For excited fans who are eager to bring the classic dwarf look and feel to AoS, this weekend marks two notable occasions. First is the wide release of the new army box set for the Khazalite holds, which offers not only a wide array of Khazalite models but also give eager fans their first chance to get their hands on the new Battletome.

Normally, we see a bit of a gap between an army box release and the wide army release, but in the case of Khazalite Holds the second wave of releases is hot on the army box’s heels, as preorders will go live on November 7th. There is an impressive number of models releasing this weekend as well, with the entire range of the faction shown off during the preview all included with the big release wave, rather than coming in a more staggered release schedule that we’ve often seen in the past.

If you’re interested in the newest Duardin face in the Mortal Realms, check out our review of the new Khazalite Holds Battletome to learn more!

Rules Updates for Age of Sigmar and Kill Team

While Warhammer 40,000’s rules update release last week was awkwardly released in little bits over several days, fans of Kill Team and Age of Sigmar lucked out and had their rules updates all drop at once last week, providing much-needed clarifications and errata for both game systems.

In the Mortal Realms, the bulk of the changes focused on the Fyreslayers and the Sons of Behemat. For the Fyreslayers, the faction keywords were updated across the board to change out the faction keyword to Khazalite, since the fiery-haired Duardin faction will be rolled into the upcoming Khazalite Holds faction, as well as updating how grudge token work in their regiment of renown. Regiments are also the main focus of the Behemat update, which introduces the new option for their Regiments of Renown to be led by Mancrusher Gargants to better accommodate 2000 point lists without dipping into Auxiliary options.

In the world of Kill Team, the highlights of the update were the changes made to TOmb World and additional errata for the Exodite Dragon Masters. For the Exodites, the new errata and rules commentary finally clears up some of the biggest lingering rules questions for the team, most importantly by making it clear just how exactly gaining cover works. As for Tomb World, multiple teams were updated so that breaching was brought in line with operate hatch for purposes of action restrictions or triggering ploys, and the pillars for Tomb World were updated to now count as cover, which opens up some very interesting new cover possibilities on Tomb World and could be a problem for shooting teams.

For more of our thoughts on the Kill Team update, check out our hot take on the changes!

Credit: BuffaloChicken

Mike Stewart Wins Telford Grand Tournament with Sylvaneth in Quiet Weekend for Events

Things were relatively quiet over the weekend for both the Age of Sigmar and Kill Team tournament scenes globally. But just because it was quiet doesn’t mean there’s nothing to cover.

While not as expansive as one of Games Workshop's marquee Open events, the new National Tournament series in the UK drew some big competition this weekend in Telford. 24 players in total battled out over five rounds, with Mike Stewart taking home the gold with an undefeated Sylvaneth list that leaned on the big heroes of the faction, including Alarielle, Drycha, and Belthanos. Mike’s win here continues a trend of very strong Sylvaneth performances in the current metagame, particularly with the big tree heroes list archetype like the one run by Mike.

As for some of the other large tournaments this weekend we have two singles events with over thirty players to look at, one in Oslo and one in Mexico. While both featured at least one Sylvaneth 4-1 player, the tree elves didn’t take home the gold at either event, with Kuba Kostrubiec’s Lumineth taking top prize at 2D6 Carnage in Oslo and Matt Nguyen winning Warhammex GT 2026 with his Slaves to Darkness. Congratulations to Mike, Matt, and Kuba for taking home the gold at their respective events!

Warmachine: Protectorate of Menoth Covenant of the Flame - Scourge of the Unbeliever

The Protectorate of Menoth Return to Warmachine

One of the most notable absences from Warmachine MK IV, the crusading zealots of the Protectorate of Menoth, finally made their triumphant return to the game last week with the release of the defenders of the flame box set, alongside standalone releases for the Revenger Light Warjack and the Crusader Heavy Warjack.

The new Protectorate of Menoth faction, the Covenant of the Flame, is led by the ambitious firebrand Feora and her closest cronies, and on the table the play much like the Protectorate of old with new twists. Like their original incarnation, Covenant of the Flame loves controlling the battlefield and setting things on fire, with the Four Gifts of Menoth army rule handing out one of four denial abilities each turn within your leaders control range to force your opponent to adjust their plans, and each leader having a unique way their army can consume fire tokens to boost their own performance and potential.

For more on the return of the Protectorate and how they were designed for the current incarnation of Warmachine, we sat down with Warmachine’s lead designer Jamie Perkins for an interview where he provided some very interesting thoughts on game design, Warmachine's appeal, and his own history with the Protectorate.

The Girls Are Fighting (You) at the MCP Fall Into the Multiverse GT

Halloween has always been one of the biggest weekends of the year for super heroes. After all, when else will you see so many Spider-Men running around the streets, on the prowl for candy?

Well this year it looks like Crisis Protocol is loathe to get left out of the fun, and hosted one of the bigger events of the weekend over at Element Games in Manchester, the Fall Into the Multiverse Official GT. This 6 round event hosted 37 players over the course of the weekend, with all corners of the Marvel universe showing up to fight for the grand prize, befitting an event named Fall Into the Multiverse.

Once the dust settled, Jim Gradwell took the top spot with his undefeated Avengers Affiliation crew that featured exclusively some of the most dangerous women in Marvel. Jim’s list, which he named “Smashing 4th walls and sometimes Matt Murdoch,” leaned exclusively on the ladies of the Avengers to draw from for his games, including She-Hulk, Captain Marvel, Wasp, Valkyrie, and Nebula, to bring home the top prize at the weekend event. Congratulations to Jim for the win!

title: Magic: The Gathering is hesitant to make Modern Horizons 4
content:
Magic: The Gathering's head designer has (more-or-less) confirmed that a new Modern Horizons set isn't currently in the works, writing on his blog that a Modern Horizons 4 set is an If, not a When.

These direct-to-modern sets have in the past been immensely popular, but also extremely controversial, and for much the same reason: they are full of powerful, format-warping cards.

While it's since been outpaced by sets like Final Fantasy and Lord of the Rings, back in 2022, Rosewater revealed that Modern Horizons 2 was the best-selling set of all time. Turns out power creep sells. As Magic has seen huge growth during this new UB era, it's likely that some of the best-performing in-universe premier sets like Tarkir Dragonstorm have now topped it too.

While they were great for Wizards' bottom line, Modern Horizons sets sparked a great deal of complaining from Modern players online. These fans were used to seeing relevant Modern cards trickle into their format gradually, as each Standard release provided perhaps one or two newcomers worth testing out.

Throwing a full 300-card release of highly relevant cards into this system was like plonking a dragon into a delicate British woodland of hedgehogs and squirrels. It upset the whole ecosystem and risked burning everything down.

For many fans, these releases removed a major reason to play a non-rotating format: that your deck, once invested in, would remain powerful and relevant for years to come.

The number of cards from Modern Horizons sets that now litter the MTG banlist is a testament to the idea that WotC may have pushed things a bit too far, and it sounds like now they're hesitant to go in this direction again. This is not the first time Rosewater has expressed this view, either. In August 2025, he mentioned off-hand that Wizards was "moving away" from direct-to-Modern sets.

On the other hand, the change in strategy may have nothing to do with the impact Modern Horizons 1, 2, or 3 had on the Modern format. It could just be that Wizards is less interested in creating cards for Constructed formats that aren't Standard. It has bigger money-makers to concern itself with these days.

Currently, it seems like Standard-legal Universes Beyond sets have more or less filled the space that might previously have been used for supplemental products like Modern Horizons - with Horizons and Remastered sets both going the way of the dodo.

Would you relish a Modern Horizons 4 or does the thought fill you with dread? Let us know over on the Wargamer Discord.

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Mycopunk
content:
When’s the last time you were killed by a microwave? For me, it was two hours ago after massacring my way through a horde of other betentacled appliances. Unfortunately, the humble microwave had been spared my full wrath and grafted the limb of a fallen comrade, which was driven into my back in vengeance.

Mycopunk is what happens when Borderlands and Deep Rock Galactic love each other very much. It is a co-op looter shooter where you take on the lethal fungi of a planet for the good of a company that is probably morally fine. Don't worry about it. You play as one of five characters with their own unique abilities. They all have some sort of movement tech and can all use the same weapons. By default, they’re quite basic because the real meat of the game is in the moment-to-moment gameplay and the upgrade system.

I Like the Way You Move

Let’s start with the gameplay. As a general rule of thumb, I value the feel of a game highly, especially movement and traversal. If controlling your character isn’t fun, the rest of the game is going to suffer as a result. Thankfully, moving around in Mycopunk is fun as hell. Deep Rock Galactic – a game very clearly in the DNA of Mycopunk – is all about claustrophobic corridors and relentless, grinding onslaughts; Mycopunk is the opposite. Missions are on wide open maps and you can absolutely haul ass through them. Even things like grinding on pipelines is noticeably faster than in comparable games.

And then there’s the vehicles. The initial vehicle, a hoverbike called the Blitseg, is like the Mass Effect Mako on meth. You don’t crash with the Blitseg, but it will always try to reorient itself to face the closest ground or ground-shaped object, so hitting a wall makes you spin wildly as you briefly go horizontal and maintain speed. Like the Mako, it requires you to be pure of heart to pilot it (there’s a definite learning curve) but once you're familiar with how it behaves, you'll have a blast going full-out and looping around jutting plateaus and boulders. To be honest, I didn’t try the other vehicles because I was having so much fun with my psychotic hoverbike.

Speaking of things that feel good, the gunplay is very satisfying. You have your basic revolver, your basic shotgun, your basic burst-fire assault rifle, your basic chainsaw, your basic plate-firing railgun… hang on.

This game accomplishes something that is genuinely hard to do; making a sci-fi arsenal that both feels high tech and is also unique. The weapons are inventive and each has its own flair. Even the generic assault rifle has a sort of spiral pattern to its bullets that makes it feel unique. And that’s all before you get into the almost six hundred upgrades that are available for both you and your guns.

Upgrading Upgrades

It is hard to make an upgrade system that feels inventive. Mycopunk pulls it off. Each upgrade is its own pattern, which you can place into a grid for each weapon and character. It turns the generic upgrade system into its own block puzzle, where builds aren’t just about the best combinations, but what combinations fit. Pigeons at Play made the very smart design decision to pair generic stat buffs with interesting gameplay changes.

Take the Glider, my personal favorite character. You can unlock the ability to move substantially fast if you glide backwards, boosting your ability to kite. In addition, that same unlock gives you a percentile increase to a stat like health or run speed. You can tech to make yourself an incredible medic who gets massive boosts to speed and strength while carrying downed players, with missiles that heal other players when they hit. Or you can have your missiles ricochet between enemies and even turn into bombs while flying.

All this frenetic gameplay does lead me to my one major complaint/word of advice. The default settings for the game turn it into a motion sickness simulator. I have legitimately never gotten motion sick from a game before, but the combination of the extremely narrow default FoV, the fisheye lens effect, and the innate head bobbing made me almost immediately nauseous. Thankfully, you can adjust these settings (though the fisheye does stay regardless; a stylistic choice that I can’t say I’m a fan of, but it certainly does make you feel more immersed in the world).

I also think the missions can become stale. The combat and progression systems keeps the game fresh, but after the tenth satellite salvage mission it felt more chore-like than I was hoping. I would have loved more story missions or a stronger guiding hand in the beginning. After the introductory mission I returned to the hub and was confused as to what I was supposed to do next because it just threw me into the full game.

Putting the Fun in Fungus

Now let’s talk about the thing that makes Mycopunk shine: the titular mycelium. The enemies in this game initially appear as generic appliances, but in reality, are the soft yellow center inside the machines. They each have random numbers and types of offensive and defensive protrusions, which you need to remove from them in order to reach that armored center. For basic enemies, you can usually just shoot them in the ‘face’, usually the screen or glass of the appliance. Alternatively, you can put enough firepower into a piece of them to blow it away and expose the center, which dies quickly once targeted.

The coolest part of all of this is the way other enemies will attach severed limbs to themselves to continue fighting. Dead Space, eat your heart out. The cartoonish art style does a lot to offset the legitimate horror of these enemies. Blow off three of the rusty metal limbs of one enemy, and it will slowly crawl towards you with the one remaining talon. All they want to do is kill. Sever the missile launching tendril of a boss and ignore it at your own peril, as one of the other weaker units will fuse with it and turn into a threat of its own. The system is genius and means combat stays fresh. Even if there are some base template enemies, anything can happen in the heat of battle and new threats can emerge. It really nails the feeling of a sentient hivemind. The individual pieces don’t matter; it will just keep growing and adapting unless you snuff out the source.

Substantive Style

The cell-shaded style and unique enemies and environments gives the game a look I’d consider ‘Charmingly Dirty’. The world is rusted, grimy, and poorly maintained; but at the same time the vibrant colors and cartoonish style makes it feel fun instead of grim. I think there is a version of this game that tries to lean into the horror aspects that are under the surface and makes the world dark both in delivery and lighting. That game would be worse than the one we have.

Indeed, every decision was made to focus on the charm of the game. Your handler, Roachard, is – as his name suggests – a cockroach, and the massive hub you spend your downtime in is filled with little jokes and world building. There’s even a projector that plays videos of other roaches engaged in everyday activities (it’s people dressed in fake roach costumes. It’s very funny).

Alongside that, the hub itself is ripe for exploration. I’m not joking about the size of the place; it took me probably a half hour to fully explore all the various rooms and minigames within.

Sometimes I’ll see games say they’re co-op between one to four players, and I’ll ask them if they mean their game is for groups-only or if you can play it solo. They’ll chuckle and say it’s a good co-op game, and then I’ll play it and see it was very clearly designed for groups. Mycopunk doesn’t have this problem. I spent a majority of my time in the game solo, and while I’m sure it would have been more fun with friends, that also describes everything that’s ever been made. Yeah, I’m playing with friends, of course it’s more fun. But the game absolutely works solo if that’s your prerogative.

Final Thoughts

Whether you’re looking for a new game for your friend-group, or just a well-made shooter to play on your own, Mycopunk delivers. While there are stronger single-player experiences out there that offer more crafted experiences, Mycopunk can absolutely go toe-to-toe with the juggernauts in the co-op looter shooter genre.

title: Warhammer: The Horus Heresy battle group value breakdown for Christmas 2026
content:
On Monday, Games Workshop revealed two different Space Marine battle group boxes for Warhammer: The Horus Heresy, each one bursting with power-armored space soldiers. While we don't yet know what Games Workshop will charge for these two sets, we've summarized what it would cost you to buy their contents separately from the Warhammer webstore, and how many points each set will contribute towards your army.

The last Horus Heresy battle group set, the Maximus box set, had an MSRP of $220 / £140. The two new sets, the Vanguard Assault Battle Group and Heavy Assault Battle Group, are slightly bigger than Maximus, so an MSRP of $250 / £165+ seems likely.

If you're building an army from scratch, the Assault Battle Group is a credible starting point for any all-rounder Space Marine Legion. The contents make a legal list right out of the box, and you can build the kits into a 1,000 point force without having to utterly load down every unit with upgrades. It's a rounded force: the Tactical Squad (or squads) are objective holders and points scorers, the Assault Squad takes objectives and scores points with its (recently buffed) Vanguard Rule, while the Contemptor Dreadnought is a durable all-rounder and the Predator provides dedicated long-ranged fire support.

The Heavy Assault Battle Group leans mostly on heavy infantry with short ranged guns, which is going to speak more to Death Guard, Iron Warriors, Salamanders, or Sons of Horus players, or to players who want to add a Zone Mortalis force to another army. Strictly speaking there are no Command models in the box, but you can run one of the six Terminators in the box as a Cataphractii Centurion, and once again you'll have a legal army in a box.

Horus Heresy is balanced around 3,000 point armies, so buying both of these boxes will get you most of the way there. However you decide to finish it, it's a list that will lean very heavily on Troops, which is a good excuse to cap off your list with a Primarch, since they all provide buffs if you go wild on Troops slots.

Of course, that assumes you aren't sitting on a huge pile of unfinished warriors from the last box set… If you're making progress through your plastic potential, why not share some pics in the Wargamer Discord community?

title: Army Rules Focus: Slaves to Darkness
content:
In this series of articles we take a deep dive into the Army Rules, or an Army of Renown, for a faction. We’ll cover the faction’s battle traits, spells, Manifestations, and upgrades as well as talk about how to build around that faction for competitive play. In this article, we’re covering the Army Rules for Slaves to Darkness.

Rules Overview

Slaves to Darkness were one of the earlier Battletomes added to the roster with the current edition, so their rules can be found readily available there or respectively in the Age of Sigmar app. All of the rules besides the seasonal Scourge of Aqshy rules are available in the tome; those can be found on the Warhammer Community website. I’ll be briefly covering those, but it’s worth mentioning that those may not be matched play legal in the future.

Battle Traits

There are two main parts to the battle traits for Slaves to Darkness (S2D): Pledges to Chaos and Eye of the Gods.

Let’s start by covering Pledges. These are the current iteration of “Marks of Chaos,” which is thematically showing each unit’s devotion to fight on behalf of a specific patron god, and being rewarded for their fervor. Once during each of your hero phases, you can select a single non-unique unit that does not already have a “Pledge to Chaos” keyword and give it one of the following abilities.

  • Pledge to Nurgle: The unit gains a 6+ ward save. If it already has one, gain a 5+ ward save.
  • Pledge to Khorne: The unit gains +1 attack to melee weapon profiles.
  • Pledge to Slaanesh: The unit gains +1 Dice to charge rolls, but must remove one dice of their choosing after the roll is made.
  • Pledge to Tzeentch: The weirdest one, fittingly. The unit gains a movement ability - Once per turn (army) in your movement phase, pick a point within 2D6 inches of your unit. Mark where that point is (this is not part of the rule, but you should do it), then pick up your unit and set it up wholly within 6” of that point and outside of 9” from enemy units.

These are all incredibly useful abilities across the entire army, and it’s important to remember that anything that isn’t a unique unit can access these, which has a lot of influence on the internal balance of the roster. There isn’t a strict priority or anything on these - we’ll cover use cases as they come up, but in general, it’s good to assume you want to try to get Khorne on your hammer units since it’s just going to be a significant damage increase on pretty much every damage unit in the army. Nurgle is great for units that already have a high wound density, like reinforced Chaos Warriors or even Ogroid Theridons. Slaanesh is interesting as it’s often more of a backup plan for when your other delivery methods fail - we’ll cover this down below when we talk about spells, but for now just treat this as a contingency plan, as it’s way better to have a unit actually succeed getting into combat and not have the Khorne pledge than the alternative. Tzeentch is great on screens or units that need a speed boost - note that it’s not a CORE ability or a Move ability, so you can pull shenanigans like using this after you move, or even using it to pseudo - retreat from combat as long as you don’t roll too low on the 2D6. This will most often be used later in games to give some more reach to your slower units or let your faster units zip across the board to a hard to snag objective.

The second part of the Army Rules is Eye of the Gods, which signifies your army leader’s attempts to earn the favor of the gods throughout the battle. During deployment, pick a single non-unique Warriors of Chaos or Darkoath hero (note this does rule out a few options, such as Ogroid Myrmidons, Centurion Marshalls, and Daemon Princes). For the rest of the battle, the unit gains Dark Apotheosis points for doing specific actions: D3 whenever they use a fight ability, and D3 at the end of each of your turns if they’re contesting an objective wholly outside of your territory.

When your selected unit reaches 8 or more Dark Apotheosis points, they can use the Dark Apotheosis ability, which is restricted to Once Per Battle (Army). They then can pick one of the following options:

  • Aura of Chaos: Heal all damage points allocated to them, then gain a 5+ ward for the rest of the battle.
  • Daemonhood: Ascend to a Daemon Prince - this has a bunch of extra stipulations, but in short, you replace the model with a Daemon Prince that gains any enhancements your original model had and must be assigned a Pledge of Chaos if the model it replaces didn’t have one. It’s worth mentioning that damage points don’t carry over to the Daemon Prince, so it effectively heals the model as well.

More often than not you’ll see this used for the Daemon Prince, but both options are solid. It’s not something that will come up naturally in every game as sometimes you just won’t hit the threshold due to dice rolls or fast combats, but it’s very handy to have when it comes up. Due to the requirements for how these points are earned, you’ll pretty much only see this on combat-oriented characters and often not on things like Sorcerer Lords.

Slaves to Darkness Chaos Lord. Credit: Loxi

Battle Formations

To be transparent, the battle formations for this army are not anything to write home about. Often you’ll be defaulting to one of them because it’s just what fits your army best, not necessarily something you’ll intentionally build around.

Godswrath Warband is what you’ll most commonly see for lists, as it’s pretty generally applicable even though it’s not super impactful. Once per turn at the end of your turn, pick an objective contested by any friendly units and put a Defiled token on it. Then do roll a D3 for each enemy unit contesting any objective that’s defiled. On a 2+, they take that many mortal wounds. It’s not a stellar ability or anything, but it’s basically just the free opportunity for extra mortals just for playing the game normally. Most importantly, it doesn’t require you to soup in anything with a Warriors of Chaos focused roster.

Darkoath Horde is arguably the best one, but is locked specifically to Darkoath heavy builds. Once per turn in your movement phase, you can activate this ability as long as you have a Darkoath hero on the battlefield. You can pay a command point to bring back a destroyed unit at half strength, wholly within 6” of a board edge outside of 3” of enemy units. This gives a ton of extra staying power to Darkoath, and ever since it became consistent (it previously was free to use, but only triggered on a dice roll) it’s become a staple of how you want to actually keep Darkoath on the board.=

Despoilers has been recently updated, and is now a very potent selection if you want to run a Daemon Prince. At the end of your turns, your Daemon Prince can pick a unit ww 12” to give them his Pledge to Chaos, replacing an existing one if they have one. This is a great way to boost your pledge economy and can make him a great pairing with anvil units like the new Aqshy Chaos Warriors, handing out Pledge to Nurgle without sacrificing damage elsewhere.

Legion of Chaos is the soup formation. While there is both at least one Warriors of Chaos hero and one Daemon or Darkoath hero on the battlefield, add 2 to the control scores of friendly Slaves to Darkness units contesting objectives wholly outside of your territory. This isn’t worth the formation slot, 2 control is just not enough to matter.

Heroic Traits

These are actually some decent options, all of them have a solid use case and will find a home in certain lists.

Favored of the Pantheon lets a unit start with 3 Dark Apotheosis points if you give it Eye of the Gods. Solid stuff, I’d say the least common of the three but it makes the threat of pulling a Daemon Prince out of nowhere much more real. If you aren’t sure what to take, this can be a safe and easy pick.

Deathmonger is my personal favorite. Gain the ability to fight a second time at strikes last, activated once per battle in the combat phase - just like Chosen and Varanguard. This can give a crazy amount of punching power to Ogroid Myrmidons, Karkadraks, and Lords on Daemonic Mounts. Basically any combat character can use this to make your turn that much stronger, and that’s a lot of what this army does well. It doesn’t always fit as well into brawler lists that don’t have as strong of an alpha strike component, but very often you’ll find a home for this.

Radiance of Dark Glory is the most important one to know about as it’s absolutely crucial to helping some lists function, but many other lists won’t want it. In ANY hero phase, pick each damaged friendly unit wholly within 12” of the holder. On a 3+, Heal (1) the target. If it’s a Monster, Heal (3) instead. This is essential to keeping big boys like Archaon and Belakor alive from shooting and chip damage, and combined with the occasional rally can make them absolute nightmares to remove. It costs 20 points at the time of writing, so you often won’t take this if you don’t have specific targets in mind for it, but I’d argue that every Archaon list and most Belakor lists want a dedicated caddy for this.

Artefacts

I’m going to be blunt - the core book artefacts for this faction are just not that great. The Scourge of Aqshy options are pretty great though.

Battletome

Conqueror’s Crown subtracts 5 from the control scores of infantry while in combat with the holder. 5 is at least a decent chunk, so if you think you’re going to be brawling around objectives it can be a good contingency if you aren’t killing what you get in combat with. Typically, I’d say we’d rather just be killing what we charge, but none of the options here really help in that department anyway.

Infernal Puppet gives you a once per battle ability you can activate at the start of any turn. Pick a visible enemy wizard within 24” of the holder. Each time they use a spell during that turn, inflict D3 damage points on them. This isn’t awful and there’s always the dream of killing a squishy 2-cast wizard with this alone, but most of the time this realistically just means “deal 1-2 D3 of damage to a wizard once per game” since most people won’t not cast the turn you pop this and will instead just burn a rally beforehand if their wizard is really at risk. Also, doing nothing into matchups where your opponent is wizard-less feels rough.

Realm Warper’s Twist Rune is a weird once per game ability that lets you pick a terrain feature within 12” - if it doesn’t have obscuring, it gains that. Then, roll a die for every model (friendly and enemy) within 1” of it, and it does a mortal on a 5+. This is interesting, to say the least. What I actually think the best use-case is for this is clearing out obnoxious infantry blocks, but it’s still pretty niche. You can technically use this to make something obscuring and then walk up to it safely during your movement phase, which is neat but likely not worth your artefact spot.

Scourge of Aqshy

Rune of Murder is a once per game ability activated in any combat phase. Pick a weapon and select one of the following options:

  • Add D6 attacks to the weapon until the end of the turn.
  • The unit takes 3 mortal damage, then double the attacks of the weapon.

This pairs incredibly well with Deathmonger to make pretty much any hero that wants to be in combat that much better at it, and will often be the default choice if you’re running a combat focused character with Deathmonger anyway.

Darkflame Pendant provides a passive ability that weapons targeting the unit have a maximum damage of 1. This is great as a survivability boost, and goes a long way on things like Daemon Princes that already have a higher amount of wounds and a ward save built in. It’s a good choice for other choices like Chaos Lords on Daemonic Mount as well, since they might not always be swinging first if they’re a secondary hammer with Knights.

Aelfskin Scroll is a once per battle reaction when an enemy wizard casts a spell within 18” of the holder. You can immediately cast a spell with a value equal to that roll without using up a power level. It’s a pretty nifty trick and has some good utility, but compared to the other options it’s a bit lackluster.

Brands of the Dark Gods (Scourge of Aqshy)

These are point-costed unit upgrades that can be put on one Non-Hero Infantry unit in your army.

Brand of Apoplexy is your most common option here, granting +1 damage to all weapons at 7 Fury levels. If you have any potential to farm fury in your list, which you should, this is going to bump a lot of extra damage out of a lot of units and has crazy synergy with Scourge of Aqshy Chaos Warriors.

Brand of Unbreakable Bonds is a once per battle ability that you can use in your movement phase to teleport your unit wholly within 3” of an objective you control and not in combat, but you can’t use charge abilities for the rest of the turn. Notably this can pull you out of combat. This is nice as a trick to get a unit out of a sticky spot, but often you’re wanting to be the one getting stuck in, so this sometimes feels a bit unnecessary. It can be a neat way to fling a large block of a durable unit up the board and teleport them back to the middle after to help hold down the fort.

Brand of The Unaligned lets you remove a unit’s pledge in your hero phase and select a new one, only once per battle for each pledge option. This only works in your hero phase, but there’s definitely utility to being able to swap between Khorne/Slaanesh  when you want to be aggressive and back to Nurgle when you know you’re going to take a punch. Do note that it has been FAQ'd so you cannot take this with an Ensorcelled Banner to get cheeky and take an ensorcelled banner of one god then switch to another to try and mix and match buffs.

Ensorcelled Banners

A unique system specifically for Slaves to Darkness, these are an additional enhancement you can attach to any unit that has at least one standard bearer, and the bonus applies as long as at least one of them is alive. There are 5 total options here - one for each Chaos god, and one representing Chaos Undivided. The god-specific options will give whatever unit you assign this to the respective Pledge, meaning you can have a unit start the game with a Pledge bonus if you choose to do so. This can be really useful if you have multiple units you want to get pledged early off in the game, so keep that in mind when assessing these.

The Dread Banner is the undivided option, and also what’s currently most commonly taken. Enemy units in combat with a unit that has this banner can’t use commands. Boom. Simple, but brutally effective. Even aside from all of the other commands that can end up throwing a wrench in your plans like Power Through, just being able to turn off All Out Attack/All Out Defence is a huge power spike for both hammer and anvil units alike. Pretty much anything that can take a banner will benefit from this, and while you don’t get the benefit of Pledge economy that you do from the other options, this opens up the flexibility to not be locked in to a specific Pledge from the start of the game.

The Banner of Rage is the Khorne option, giving the unit Pledged to Khorne as well as +1 to wound rolls in melee. If you have a unit you know you want to be juiced up with a Khorne pledge anyway, this isn’t a bad choice for very “full send” oriented lists that might want to mark a lot of things early. Often turning off all out defence for effectively -1 save on your opponents can pull more weight as it’s easier to get wound bonuses in the army than rend bonuses, but this is still a reasonable option for hammer units.

The Banner of Screaming Flesh is the Slaanesh option, giving the unit Pledged to Slaanesh as well as +1 attack to melee weapons if the unit charges. While this ends up amounting to making your unit less effective in combat than just taking The Banner of Rage, it does mean you can make a really effective self-sufficient unit. With Slaanesh helping secure better charges and still getting the +1 attack you’d be missing out on from Khorne, you can throw this banner on a unit you want to drive up a flank and give them little extra support. The most common use case for this is reinforced Knights, as they can rip things up pretty well with this and nothing more.

The Eroding Icon is the Nurgle choice here, granting Pledged to Nurgle as well as making all critical hits against the unit count as normal hits instead. Ignoring Crit (Mortal) is really devastating for some units, so often this is something you take as a meta call when there are a lot of scary threats that have critical abilities. Beyond that, Nurgle is quite a good pledge to start with if you have a big reinforced anvil of some kind, as it means you can still get your combat bonuses on other things without missing out on this early.

The Blasted Standard is the Tzeentch banner, and by far the most niche one. It grants Pledged to Tzeentch as well as a 4+ ward against shooting attacks. You don’t often want big units stuck on Tzeentch from the start of the game, so this is really reserved for scenarios where shooting is a serious problem for your important stuff.

Slaves to Darkness Chaos Lord. Credit: Loxi

Spell Lore

Our spell lore is categorized by having some very powerful spells with pretty restricted casting ranges. Everything has a 12” range, so be ready to get pretty close to what you want to target.

Spite-Tongue Curse is our unlimited spell, it casts on a 5 which is actually really consistent. Pick an enemy within 12”, then make your casting roll. If it’s successful, 3 mortals to the target, no extra dice rolls needed. If it’s unsuccessful or unbound, the caster takes D3 mortals. This spell is alright, in some matchups the unbinds can hurt quite a bit and really end up adding up in chip damage. The plus side is that it’s a very consistent mortal output spell, and even though the range is short, it’s one of the few ways we have to project damage outside of melee range. It’s not the reason you bring wizards, but it’s helpful to have in your pocket.

Daemonic Speed is your bread and butter buff spell, and one of the huge benefits to taking a wizard here. Casting on a 7, target a unit wholly within 12” of the caster. If successful, add 1 to the number of dice rolled when making charge rolls. This is the juice. This is how you can more reliably deliver things like Chosen, Theridons, and other things that are a bit slower than the rest of your force exactly where you need them. You can also use this to just give your already fast units a truly absurd threat range.

Binding Damnation is your last trick, casting on a 7. Select an enemy unit within 12”, and if the cast is successful they get Strikes Last until the start of your next turn. Powerful, but as with the other spells here, the range means you do have to be reasonably close to get this off. That being said, if you’re casting this on your own turn and don’t take a double, this is two full combats worth of Strike Last goodness. This is a combat focused army, so being able to mess with combat order can be great - the biggest issue here being that unlike other similar combat tricks, this happens so early in the turn that you won’t really be using this unless you’re already pretty stuck in.

Manifestations

Friends, I have terrible news here. Manifestations of Malevolence, the faction-specific manifestations for S2D, are just really bad. You gain an inconsistent shooting attack that can’t even shoot the turn you place it because the range is too short, an extremely conditional and finicky attack bonus aura, and a mediocre hoard clearing piece. Unless your local meta is just loaded with chaff lists, these are absolutely not worth considering at the time of writing.

There is great news however - we make fantastic use of the other manifestation lores. While some of them cost points to include, these costs are absolutely worth it and should pretty much always be prioritized over the default faction choice.

Forbidden Power is often the default choice, as it’s extremely useful across the board. Soulscream bridge gives us some much needed mobility for our infantry, and paired with Pledge to Slaanesh or, better yet, Daemonic Speed, this can give some serious reach to units that are stuck with slower movement. Shards of Valagharr provides some great backfield screening, and Horrorghast can give a little extra shooting punch to a roster that doesn’t really have much of that. Lauchon isn’t always the most useful, but it can be handy to have in a pinch.

Primal Energy is a great pick if you’re relying on any of the centerpiece unique characters or if you aren’t really going to utilize Bridge as well from Forbidden Power. The healing is great for our monster heroes from Emerald Lifeswarm, and Jaws is always handy for extra screening and mortal damage output.

Aetherwrought Machineries is good if you’re really strapped for points or running Archaeon, as he makes fantastic use of the -1 to hit from Chronomatic Cogs. Pendulum is handy for creating space on the board, and Quicksilver Swords can be some helpful damage for assassinating targets relying on ward saves.

Twilit Sorceries is a mixed bag for us: we already have a great way to turn off commands in The Dread Banner, and protection from shooting isn’t as important for an army that plans to close the gap very fast anyway. That being said, Geminids is nice if you aren’t taking The Dread Banner, and the Umbral Spellportal can be quite helpful to mitigate our generally lower ranges for spells.

Krondspine Incarnate and Morbid Conjuration both are fine in their own rights, but don’t bring as much to the table that the other lores offer. We don’t really need more help in the fighting/damage departments, it’s getting there and staying there that is often more helpful to gain from these.

Faction Terrain

The Nexus Chaotic is quite a contentious piece of faction terrain, as it’s not bad by any means, but it’s also completely non-essential for the faction to function. 12 wounds on a 4+ save with a pretty big footprint is pretty typical, but it does mean it won’t die to chip damage and often does require at least some degree of commitment to kill. In each of your hero phases, you can roll a die and add that many power points to it, up to a maximum of 12. You can then spend those points on the following abilities:

Infernal Sorcery costs 3 points, and gives a friendly Slaves to Darkness wizard within 3” of the terrain feature +1 to casting rolls for the turn. Great for setting up Bridge/Daemonic Speed on early turns, and even better on 2-cast characters like Archaon, Belakor, and the Gaunt Summoner.

Corrupt the Realms costs 9 points, and requires you to select an objective or terrain feature within 24” of the Nexus. Any number of enemies within 3” are the targets. Roll a D3 for each unit, and on a 2+ deal that many mortals. This is fine, it’s basically free damage to midfield targets that will happen semi-randomly since you can’t really always rely on having the power points.

If you’re able to make use of both of these, it’s a solid piece and definitely worth deploying. You won’t really be getting the casting bonus after the first turn or two in most matchups, but setting up your early spells better is pretty handy, even though it’s not 100% reliable. The mortal wounds can be helpful, but it’s not often going to make or break your gameplan. As a good rule of thumb, if your opponent has a ton of teleporting/high mobility shenanigans and you aren’t making use of the casting bonus, you can consider leaving this off the board to not give a stationary target for people to charge off. It’s 0 opportunity cost to bring in a list though, so it’s worth always packing it.

Chaos Warriors. Credit: SRM

Tricks and Combos

There are a whole ton of tricks and synergies to cover, so I’m just going to rapid fire mention a bunch of them. Keep in mind this is not a comprehensive list of every little thing with the army - these are just touching on some of the topics covered above.

  • Sequencing your abilities is one of the most important things you can do here. Always try to cast Daemonic Speed and/or Soulscream Bridge before you assign your Pledge to Chaos - if you successfully get one of these buffs on a unit, you can opt for something like Pledge to Khorne to get more damage, but if you’re unsuccessful and still have a sketchy charge, you can instead choose Pledge to Slaanesh to make sure they still get in.
  • Magical Intervention is a very useful tool here: setting up Soulscream bridge can be handy, and even if your opponent wastes time walking up to destroy it, that can often be just as helpful to close the gap more.
  • This is more generic to Soulscream Bridge, but for those unaware it can be very useful for movement blocking, as you can move through manifestations but can’t end up on top of them, so it can take up a lot of space on a unit’s flank to make charges awkward.
  • Varangard can’t have a standard bearer, so if you’re running them and another big hammer unit that you want to send out early, having a banner that conveys a Pledge to Chaos can be invaluable as you really want to make sure Varangard are marked when they go to fight.
  • Your Daemon Princes that come into play via Dark Apotheosis get to pick if they have wings for FLY and +2” movement or a Trophy Rack for +1 rend against heroes. Don’t sleep on the trophy rack here, a Nurgle Daemon Prince with a Trophy Rack can brawl with a lot of tough cookies.
  • Radiance of Dark Glory isn’t that big of an aura - 12” can be finicky if you’re trying to heal something with a big base like Archaon. To help with this, try to put it on something else with a big base if possible - Chaos Lord on Daemonic Mount and even the Centurion Marshall are good choices for this purpose alone.
  • The Dread Banner often makes a lot of sense to put on a unit with a lot of staying power like Reinforced Chaos Warriors if you’re playing a more traditional “hammer and anvil” playstyle, as your Hammers will frequently be fighting near them anyway.

title: Hobby Build Academy: How to Handle a Backlog
content:
Welcome back to Hobby Build Academy, where your professors Marcy and Elly explore the world of hobby model kit building and all of the ups and downs that come with it. We've been focusing on building out tools, useful things to have, and reviewing kits as we build them, but perhaps keen readers have noticed something: We haven't had many model reviews lately! Well, we'll talk a bit about why that is, and that also gave us the time to talk about something that seems to always circle hobby activities: the dreaded backlog. But is a backlog actually a bad thing, and how best to think about it regardless of the answer?

Faculty Lounge

This guy WILL be built.

Marcy: So, I think it isn't such a bad idea to open up this week's talk with some of the reasons as to why we've had a little lull in actual model building as of late; if anything, I think it's a great way to explore the fact that backlogs can build up very quickly, and also that a lot of things that we can't control often play a big role in them. I see people talk about them from the perspective of laziness or personal failure, but I think the actual reality is that our hobbies tend to always play a secondary role that, unfortunately, tends to get forced to the sideline.

Elly: Yeah... so, I haven't talked about it much here, but I suffer from a few chronic illnesses, which tend to greatly impact my available energy and focus. That tends to mean I have to prioritize my work first, and my other activities second, otherwise there's a chance I won't get things done that absolutely need to get done. And, well, I have a lot of interests, but also what energy I have left can sometimes be pretty variable too. On days when I have a lot of energy, I might prefer to go out or be more active, and in others, I might prefer to relax and read or play a game. Models have been... kind of an interesting challenge.

Marcy: For myself, I tend to be juggling a lot of things and spinning a lot of plates, so my downtime is generally pretty restricted. Actually, one of the reasons we started this column and this hobby together was to have something we specifically do together that isn't just an overlap of our interests, but something we do together. So, this means that when your energy isn't where it needs to be when my time is free, or the opposite, it can make working on things together difficult.

Elly: Then there's the attention and focus, which are... another problem, hah.

Marcy: Yeah. And I don't think there's much wrong with talking about that either; while you can have a larger struggle reigning in both of those, my focus can by laser pointed, but that doesn't mean I have the time to engage with things.

Elly: Which is to say, there's been some other things going on too.

Marcy: Yeahhhhhhhh. After September ended, we had picked up quite a few new models, as the end of the month is my birthday, so we'd gone on a bit of a trip to get some new kits, and also attended the model show. Unfortunately, that got tied with an increase in my work schedule and a decrease in my downtime, but also my car suffered a pretty huge need for repair, which took a lot of my time, energy, and focus (as well as money) to circumvent.

Elly: So, on the bright side, we have a lot of models to build, but also, on the down side, we have... a lot of unbuilt models. And actually, I have one that's incomplete, because we were working on a new set of kits before things kind of snowballed and I hadn't had the time or energy to get back to finishing it.

Marcy: Right! So, now that our personal preamble is out of the way, let's talk about backlogs themselves; if anything, we mostly thought talking about ours and how it got created so fast so openly would be relatable, since there's often a problem with recognizing that it isn't very hard to amass one, thinking that they just sneak up or appear due to other factors.

Back to Backlogs

This guy, also, will be built. Eventually.

Marcy: So, a backlog, for anyone blissfully unaware of them, is a term used for a "pile" of figurative, or literal, projects or items that generally have built up over a period of time and inactivity. You'll sometimes hear about people joking about their Steam backlogs, for example, so it isn't that they have to huge physical piles of unbuilt models or minis, but in reality, it just has to be a set of things that keep getting forgotten and possibly added to over time.

Elly: Yeah... which can be hell on one's mental health when it comes to hobbying. The sense of guilt about a backlog can really create a pretty negative cycle in your head: "I didn't finish that, I guess I won't finish it, I feel bad for not finishing it," which can just keep taking those projects to further and further lengths of being unfinished. I know I've certainly had this problem myself so far, where I keep feeling like because I didn't finish a kit, I've become guilty of some sort of thing and it makes it harder to stay motivated to get back in. It sounds irrational as I write it out, but I think it might be relatable...

Marcy: No, I think it absolutely is; there's a lot of times in which something that hasn't been completed, just out of eye sight or concentration, starts building up some level of weight on its own that somehow being unfinished is a reminder. Something you didn't do, or finish, or complete.

Elly: The other thing with backlogs is that there's no real size to them; if anything, a single item that hasn't been interacted with can be a backlog! They don't all have to be mountains of grey plastic and shrink wrapped boxes. For us, we've got about ten models between us now that need to be built before we could consider our backlog emptied.

Marcy: Yeah, and... honestly, I could add a few more things to that. I have a Transformers LEGO kit that I haven't gotten around to working on that's been about a year now, for example, so... sometimes a backlog goes from 1, to 5, to 10! But at least ours is shared, so 10 isn't really as bad as it sounds in terms of gunpla.

Elly: I'd say that as we talked about backlogs, something that seemed to come to mind is that it doesn't really matter how big or small it is, or how it came to be, just that it exists, and that it existing can create further problems when it goes too long without being completed.

Managing a Backlog

And THIS one! We actually did track one down!

Marcy: So, in considering how to deal with a backlog, there isn't really a single magical answer that we can provide. Obviously, these are things that we know work for us, and are mostly just sharing them as ways to consider or think about them that might help turn something that seems insurmountable into something that can actually be conquered.

Elly: So, obviously, "just do it" is a simple answer, but it rarely is actually as easy as it seems. If "just do it" was that effective a mindset, people wouldn't have backlogs or other things stumbling their way otherwise. That said, there is some merit to actually setting yourself up to succeed when you fall behind on projects. As we were talking, the idea that "guilt" can keep you from finishing things really does become something that can get in the way of making progress. "I can do it later, I've already failed to do it" is a mindset, and so setting an actual time, making a promise or other sort of commitment, is probably the first, best step to getting real progress to happen.

Marcy: For me, that's generally how I approach my writing. I always try to write a few hundred words a day at least, if not a few thousand, and I developed that primarily because I stalled out on my PhD. years ago and realized if I didn't set something into a routine, I'd never finish it; ever since, I just keep at it like I would anything else. Making it into a routine, a thing that I keep up with, helped make my writing easy but also consistent. For hobbying, frankly, I actually still have the same problem; hobbying isn't something I have to do for my daily life to function, so it becomes really, really easy to forget about things.

Elly: Another thing we discussed is tackling projects in orders of magnitude. We have a few new kits, but of them, there are some RG and MG kits, but also a few SD kits, and so far our "return" to working on kits will likely be the SD kits. A smaller project that works with your backlog might just be an easy first step; I definitely know from other projects I've fallen behind on that trying to tackle the absolute biggest thing on the list often ends up as a mistake.

Marcy: Yeah, back when I was painting miniatures, I certainly fell into that trap a lot. Figuring that I'd become burnt out on smaller models and boring details, I kept trying to work off of larger, detailed projects, which only served to deepen my sense of guilt over not finishing things, as bigger models were harder to stay engaged with on my schedule. Sadly, I have a half painted zombie dragon to attest for that...

Elly:I think the hardest part of a backlog to wrestle with is... sometimes, you just have to admit that you've moved on. Thankfully we didn't reach that point with gunpla, or this column would stop existing, but I know both of us have had that in the past with other hobbies. When you realize that you are just actually never going to tackle those projects, it may not be because of not finding the time, it may just be that a loss of passion or interest has turned that "pile of shame" into a "pile of disinterest".

Marcy: Yep. And when that happens, it really does become time to be honest with yourself: sometimes, the best thing you can do is get rid of your backlog, literally. Selling, trading, or otherwise offloading your backlog to other people is a great way to actually remove a sense of guilt over the things you haven't finished. It can also help remove the monetary sense of guilt that a backlog creates too; by selling or trading the things you've really lost interest in, it can also alleviate a sense that you've wasted money too.

Elly: I do think it's the last resort, obviously. You don't want to rush to sell something, only to then realize you actually were just going to get to it eventually and have to re-buy it again!

Marcy: Overall, I do think there's no real answer to backlogs; we certainly aren't going to sit here and pretend we know how to prevent them. But, maybe some of this will help mange them. I don't think they're something to be ashamed of, just that letting them grow and grow is irresponsible. By actually taking steps to mitigate or approach the backlog, it becomes something that you can actually get rid of, rather than just "tolerate" as being out of sight, out of mind. We do hope to be back with builds soon, because we've got a few really cool kits we're excited to show off!

title: Japanese D&D killer Sword World RPG nears $3 million on crowdfunder
content:
The Backerkit campaign for the first ever official English language edition of Sword World RPG, the first and longest-running Japanese TTRPG, has raised over $2,800,000 at time of writing, with 18 days to go. Sword World was originally published in 1989, and completely displaced Dungeons and Dragons as Japan's premier fantasy RPG.

The crowdfunding campaign is for the "complete localization, design, and printing of the Sword World 2.5 Core Rules" in English. A pledge for the holy trinity of Core Rulebook, Monster Manual, and Gamemaster's Guide, in both hardback and PDF, plus a slipcase and DM's screen, costs $175 (£130), while the core rulebook alone is $55.

Japanese TTRPGs often have more boardgame-like components and handouts than Western ones, and the optional add-ons are accordingly packed with bling. The campaign runs until November 20, and is expected to ship around the end of 2027 - you can find the full details on Backerkit.

Sword World is a classic fantasy RPG, but optimised around a different set of design goals from D&D, particularly modularity, and telescoping design. The core resolution system is a 2D6 roll, adding any modifiers from skills, and comparing against a target number. Then there are Power Tables, lookup tables that turn the result of a 2D6 roll into a range of other values, to give you combat damage numbers. The full Power Table has 50 different power levels for attacks, but the progression is subtle, and it's quite normal to use only every fifth power level.

There are three different resolution levels for combat as well. In the simplest mode characters are assigned to the front row (for melee) or back row (for support), like a turn-based JRPG. The most complex mode uses full grid-based movement. The standard combat mode sits in-between them, using a single distance axis to track how near or far characters are from the middle of the fight.

Though the rules are the same as 2018's 2.5 edition, these are otherwise completely original books; Japanese text takes so much less space than English that it would be impossible to just "swap out" the languages and reuse the old graphic design. The art and design of the English editions is being directed by Shunsuke Nakashige, the director of hit anime Solo Levelling, with new art from long-time Sword World illustrator Hitoshi Yoneda.

Sword World has been continuously published by Group SNE for 35 years, and the game is only on edition 2.5. Assuming the game launches successfully in English - and the crowdfunding total suggests it could well do - there are a lot of Japanese supplements waiting to be localized into English. I've got my fingers crossed that everything goes well!

I interviewed the mom and pop duo who are translating Sword World and publishing it via their company Mugen Gaming, Ai and Shawn Namima-Davison, this spring. They provided me with a detailed history of how the Sword World RPG developed out of the D&D campaign write-up series turned fantasy novelization Record of Lodoss War, as well as some incredible insights into the challenges of translating the game - you can find the interview here.

title: Contemptor Kevin's Combat Patrol Issue 72 Review
content:
Not every issue of Combat Patrol is going to have the most scintillating selection of Hobby Materials. After all, we've had several issues filled with Genestealer Cults Infantry. Unfortunately, Issue #72 is a paint issue and we are only now reviewing it on Halloween 2026. However, while the actual hobby materials this issue comes with are sub-optimal, the contents of this issue do their best to make up for it. So what's going on here? Let's find out! As always, thank you to TabletopBattles and Hachette for the opportunity to review these paints, magazines, and materials.

Hobby Materials

The elephant in the room is that this is a paint issue that has two Warhammer Paint layer paints: White Scar and Yriel Yellow. White Scar is a venerable thinner/less pigmented white paint, while Yriel Yellow is a bright warm yellow, much more vibrant than the subscription's yellow base paint, Warhammer Paint Averland Sunset. I own several of these paints, and one pot of Yriel Yellow recently exploded in a paint bag. Why am I so down on these paints, then?

Because we live in the age of Warhammer Tone Pro, and there is a TonePro equivalent to both paints. While I personally do not own the specific paint, Joseph "CrabstuffedMushrooms" Knoblauch has made it his goal to try and test every TonePro paint that he can. And Joey tells me that Hawkshroud Yellow 2 is a match for Yriel Yellow. As I believe every reader of this website knows now, Blackstone Void 5 rendered every single previous Warhammer Paint white obsolete. So while these paints were perfectly cromulent when the issue came out, they have since been supplanted by better TonePro paints that are easier to use.

Necromunda Fixer painted by CrabstuffedMushrooms, where he took Hawkshroud Yellow 2 and Blackstone Void 5 out for a spin.

And the magazine's Paint Guide is fantastic for how to use Blackstone Void 5 and Hawkshroud Yellow 2 on previously painted miniatures. The article has us use White Scar to highlight and edge highlight the whites and light grey portions of such miniatures like the Terminators' helmets and Crux Terminatuses, use Yriel Yellow on Tyranid eyes and Genestealer Cult mechanics, and Warhammer Paint Administratum Grey to edge highlight various black materials.

Base primed with White Scar Spray. Top half is Yriel Yellow. Bottom Half is Hawkshroud Yellow 2. Main difference is the latter has extremely smooth application. Credit: Kevin Stillman

The issue gives good advice and strategies for painting your minis! The only downside is that there's now better paints that make it easier to edge highlight Warhammer minis.

Narrative Materials

We return to the Silver Templars' Squad Askarton in Bonds of Honour, Part 17. In Part 16, the Space Marines successfully defeated an Ork warboss and a bunch of Orks. As thanks for the assist, the Kin of the Leagues of Votann gave Squad Askarton a lift off-planet. The Kin dropped the Marines off at an Imperial world, to which Squad Askarton hoped to hitchhike their way further through the galaxy. Unfortunately, instead of being dropped off at an operating spaceport, the Kin dropped them off in "some shattered urban wasteland". This didn't bother the Marines overmuch, but Sergeant Askarton still wanted to find his missing Bolt Rifle. So they fired off a vox signal for help. The squad was located by a platoon of the Imperial Guard, who were investigating the appearance of a xenos ship. Unfortunately, the Guardsmen had not actually seen a Space Marine before and were scared. Sergeant Askarton removed his helmet to conduct diplomacy with the Guard, but Sergeant Askarton was an uggo and taking off his helmet scared the Guardsmen even further. One brave Guardswoman decided to step forward and was promptly shot in the head. The rest of the Guard blamed the Space Marines, and unloaded their weapons at the Astartes. The Astartes took cover, and waited for the Guard to exhaust their weapons. Once the Guard finish wasting their ammunition, the real hammer blow falls.

Ankran Mechanised Imperial Guards. Credit: Charlie Brassley

We then get narrative articles about the Guard. The first is about the Combined Arms nature of the Guard. The Imperial Guard usually use combined-arms regiments, which mix artillery, heavy weapons, armored vehicles, and schmucks. They also have special forces detachments, and aircraft in the form of Valkyrie Assault Carriers. The Astra Militarum is the symbol of humanity's resolve, as it is how humanity resists Chaos cults, Chaos Legions, the foulest xenos, and everything else.

Lastly, we get another map of the galaxy with active Astra Militarum warzones. The first two, Thyriss Paterna and Norada VII, are "redacted", while the third is Vigilus. We have several other battlezones, such as Rafnar Sub-4c where insurrectionist mining guides are defeated but now an "unknown foe battles against Imperial troops in the cramped mine workings", Gorentz (Where the Orks are having a happy time), and Orvastan Planus (Tyranids).

Gaming Materials

I've mentioned before that the Hachette Combat Patrol magazine is fairly cynical towards the Imperium of Man in their narrative sections, and nowhere is this more evidence than in the gaming materials of this section. We have two Crusade missions, and the first is Astra Militarum versus Space Marines. As if trying to recreate the battle from Bonds of Honour Part 17, we have the Astartes seeking archaeotech and telling the Guard to keep the Marine mission quiet. Unfortunately, Guard command is a mess and so the Marines just opt to wipe out the Guard in order to leave no survivors.

The second mission is the Guard having to fight the Tyranids, because the Tyranids want to eat everything and the Guard want to dissuade the Tyranids from trying to eat them.

The Final Verdict

The materials in this magazine are, bluntly, a lot of fun. We rarely get unity between the gaming scenario and the narrative scenarios at this point in Combat Patrol, and the gaming scenario reflects the cynicism of the author. I was not expecting this level of fun from the narrative section when writing this while handing out trick-or-treat candy!

The magazine's hobby material section is also quite nice, explaining where to make final touch highlights that give miniatures an bright, extra pop. Where the issue runs into some value trouble, of course, is that the paint issues are usually the weaker bargains from Combat Patrol. On top of that, GW has since introduced a new paint range that specifically obsoletes this issues two paints. So if you are only buying this magazine for the bargains...you can get pots of Blackstone Void 5 and Hawkshroud Yellow 2 for cheaper than this issues' MSRP. Luckily, next week we're back to our regularly scheduled model issues.

Until next time Combat Patrolers!

title: Does this Pokémon card reveal dash hopes for Mega Blastoise?
content:
Last week, when The Pokémon Company accidentally revealed its plans for next year's McDonald's promotion, the one brand new card that leaked sparked a lot of interest. That's because it was an unseen Squirtle - presumably one from a soon-to-release Pokémon TCG set. And that was exciting because fans were hoping it would herald the long-awaited arrival of Mega Blastoise to the game.

After all, Mega Charizard has had both its forms appear in the Mega Evolution era. Mega Venusaur, too, was featured in its very first set. Only the cannon-toting turtle lacks representation - an injustice we should not stand for!

This new Squirtle card could be there as support for Mega Blastoise, a new basic Pokémon to evolve into the water type Mega. However, a new spoiler for Japan's November (our February) set Aura Seeker shows that regular Blastoise is in this release.

This Blastoise card is almost certainly designed with the new Squirtle in mind, as well. It has an ability which states that attacks dealt to the bench by water Pokémon do 30 more damage. Meanwhile Squirtle's Splatter attack hits the bench - the synergy is obvious.

We can't rule out the possibility that both Blastoise and Mega Blastoise will feature in the Aura Seeker/Flowing Fists release. After all, we're a long way from seeing the full list of cards. Only three megas have been revealed thus far - the Z Mega forms for Lucario, Absol, and Garchomp - and that won't be all of them. Even the smallest sets like Chaos Rising have had about five.

If there is a Mega Blastoise in this set, we can assume it will have some sort of bench-targeting attack to play well with its mini-me form. Then again, perhaps regular Blastoise is in there as support for Mega Starmie, which can already wallop the bench.

What do you think - does the new Blastoise make Mega Blastoise less likely or more? Let me know over on the Wargamer Discord. I feel it could go either way!
